notes.meaning: After John wrote down the letters to the seven churches, he saw a new vision. A door into heaven was already standing open. The same trumpet-like voice he heard in chapter 1, the voice of Christ, called him up to be shown what would happen in the future. We can know the future only as far as God chooses to open the door.

differ.view: Some see John being called up as a picture of the rapture. That is the belief that the church will be caught up to meet Christ before a time of great trouble on earth. They note that the word "church" does not appear again until much later in the book.
Others say this is only John being invited into heaven in his vision, not the rapture. John went up "in the Spirit," and his body stayed on the island of Patmos.

notes.meaning: Right away John was "in the Spirit." God's Spirit took hold of him in a vision. The first thing he saw was a throne in heaven, and it was not empty. The One sitting on it is God the Father, ruling as King and Judge, and every earthly throne is under His.

John does not describe God's face or shape. He describes only a shining brightness, like precious stones: clear, gleaming jasper and deep red carnelian. Many writers see the brightness as God's holiness and the red as His justice. The green rainbow around the throne recalls God's promise to Noah, a sign of mercy wrapped around God's power to judge.

Around God's throne were twenty-four smaller thrones, with elders seated on them. Many commentators believe these elders stand for all of God's people, both Old and New Testament believers. They may be pictured as the twelve tribes of Israel and the twelve apostles. Their white clothes speak of purity and the right standing God gives them, and their gold crowns speak of victory and honor.

differ.view: Some believe the elders are the church already taken up to heaven in the rapture. They point out that angels are never called elders or promised crowns.
Some think the elders are most likely a high rank of angels who surround God's throne, though they may also represent believers.

notes.meaning: Lightning and thunder came from the throne, just as they did when God gave the law at Mount Sinai. They show God's great power and majesty, and His power to judge. The seven burning torches are "the seven Spirits of God." Most writers take this to mean the one Holy Spirit in all His many works, giving light and life and making God's people pure.

differ.view: Some take the seven torches to be seven angels who serve before God's throne.

notes.meaning: Before the throne was something like a sea of glass, clear as crystal. Earthly seas are stormy, but this one is calm and still, a picture of God's pure and peaceful rule. Some link it to the big washbasin in the temple, called a "sea," where priests washed before serving God. Around the throne were four "living creatures" like the cherubim (mighty angels) Ezekiel saw, and their many eyes show that nothing escapes God's notice.

Each creature looked different. One was like a lion, one like a young ox, one had a man's face, and one was like a flying eagle. Many writers say these are the noblest of their kinds: the lion over wild animals, the ox over tame animals, the eagle over birds, and man at the head of all. Together they picture the very best of God's creation.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: From the early church onward, the four creatures became symbols of the four Gospel writers, Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. Early writers did not agree on which creature went with which Gospel. These symbols became standard in Christian art.

notes.meaning: Each creature had six wings, like the angels Isaiah saw, and was covered with eyes inside and out. They never stop praising God. They say "Holy" three times, because God is completely pure and set apart, far above everything He made. He is the Almighty, who always was, is now, and is still to come.

Whenever the living creatures give glory to God, the twenty-four elders join in. They fall down, worship, and throw their crowns before the throne. This shows that every honor they have came from God, so they gladly give it back to Him. Our own praise should be like theirs: humble, thankful and constant.

The elders sing that God is worthy of all glory, honor and power. The reason is that He created everything. All things exist only because He willed it, and He keeps them going. Since God alone is the Creator, He alone should be worshiped.
